name: SPSS
intro_md:
Most quantitative theses still run their numbers in SPSS, and most of the work is not the clicking. It is reading the output, knowing which figure passes, and knowing what to do when one does not.

The posts here follow the order you actually meet the procedures in: entering and cleaning the data, coding and reverse-coding items, descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation, linear regression, then the difference tests, independent samples t-test and one-way ANOVA. Each post stops at one procedure. It gives the menu path, walks through every table the procedure prints, and states the cut-off it uses together with the source that cut-off comes from, because a threshold with no citation is the first thing a reader asks about.

A good share of the posts deal with things going wrong, since that is where the time goes. An item that has to be dropped because its factor loading sits under the acceptable value. A rotated component matrix that will not settle into the structure your model assumed. A significance value above 0.05 on the one hypothesis the whole study was built around. Those are the points a supervisor asks about at the defence, and they are also the points a paid analysis service tends to leave undocumented. The aim is that you can run the analysis yourself, explain the output, and not pay for a table of numbers you cannot defend.

If your model has mediators, moderators, or more latent constructs than a regression will carry, read the SmartPLS category as well. If you do not have data yet, the Surveys category covers sample size and instrument design, which are decisions no amount of work in SPSS will fix afterwards.

Where to start. If your data is entered but nothing has been run, read the post on cleaning and coding first, then descriptive statistics, which gives you the sample profile table your results chapter opens with. After that, follow the real run order: Cronbach's alpha, EFA, correlation, regression. Read the post on the Coefficients table and the one on what a significance value does and does not tell you before writing a single sentence about a hypothesis. The troubleshooting posts are worth reading when you hit the specific problem they describe, and not before.

name: Statistics
intro_md:
A quantitative thesis uses perhaps twenty statistical ideas, but they turn up on every page and most of them are half understood: standard deviation, variance, the median, outliers, the p-value, correlation coefficients, confidence intervals, sample size.

Each post here takes one concept and answers the questions a thesis writer actually has about it. What it measures. How it is calculated, with a worked example small enough to check by hand. Which column it appears in when SPSS or SmartPLS prints it. And what counts as an acceptable value in social science research, which is not the same answer as in a laboratory. Every post ends with a paragraph on how to state that result in the results chapter, because knowing a coefficient is 0.68 and knowing how to write the sentence about it are two different skills.

A sensible reading order runs from describing data, to distribution and outliers, and only then to inference: p-values, hypothesis tests, and confidence intervals. If a reviewer has asked why you used 0.05 rather than 0.01, or why you reported a median instead of a mean, the answer is here rather than in a software manual.

Software procedure sits in the SPSS and SmartPLS categories so the posts here can stay on what the number means. Some overlap is deliberate: the reliability post here explains what internal consistency is, and the SPSS post shows you where to click.

Where to start. If you have just collected data, read the post on descriptive statistics so you can describe your sample with frequencies, means, and standard deviations. Then read the posts on normality and on outliers, because those two decide whether you are allowed to use parametric tests at all, and that decision belongs before any hypothesis test rather than after one comes out badly. Read the post on the p-value before you run anything, so that a small number does not get written up as a large finding. Finish with correlation and with sample size, the two concepts a committee is most likely to ask you to defend out loud.

name: Surveys
intro_md:
Bad data cannot be rescued by good analysis. A scale that does not hold together, a leading question, a sample that is too small, and responses filled in without reading all surface at the reliability and factor analysis stage, by which point the fieldwork is over and there is nothing to be done.

This category runs from questionnaire design to a clean data file: choosing how many points your Likert scale needs, writing items for each construct so that each one measures a single thing, calculating sample size from the number of indicators and from the analysis you intend to run, distributing online, screening out invalid responses, and coding the result for import.

The posts are direct about the parts that go wrong. Response rates that come in well under what the sampling plan assumed. Reverse-worded items that confuse careful respondents more than they catch careless ones. Missing data, and the difference between dropping a case and imputing a value. Where a post gives a formula it names the source of that formula rather than presenting a number as settled.

If you would rather have an instrument distributed and cleaned than build that step by hand, some posts mention survify.net. That is our own product rather than a third-party recommendation, and every post that mentions it says so.

Once you have a usable file, the SPSS category picks up at reliability testing. The Research models category is the one to read first if you are still deciding which constructs the questionnaire has to measure at all.

Where to start. Read the post on Likert scales first, because the number of points decides how you word every item and how you code the responses later. Sample size next, and read it before you distribute rather than after, since too few cases is the one error no analysis will fix. The questionnaire design post covers item order, reverse-worded items, and screening questions. When the responses are in, the posts on response screening and on coding for SPSS take you to a file that is ready for Cronbach's alpha.

name: Research methods
intro_md:
A student research project or a first paper differs from a thesis in one way that matters: it has to stand in front of a reviewer who does not know you and has no reason to be generous. The research question has to be specific, the method has to be defensible on its own terms, and the results have to claim only what the data supports.

This category covers the shape of a quantitative study end to end: identifying a problem worth researching, turning it into a research question, reading and organising the literature, deriving hypotheses from theory rather than from intuition, choosing a design, collecting and analysing data, and writing it up. The posts on research design, on primary and secondary data, on the difference between qualitative and quantitative work, and on independent, dependent, mediating and control variables all sit here.

DoThesis supports quantitative work with surveys and statistics only. So when a post compares qualitative and quantitative approaches, the purpose is to help you see which one your question calls for and why, not to teach interview technique or thematic coding. If your question needs interviews, this is the wrong toolkit, and the post will say so rather than talk you into a survey.

If you already have a topic and want to go straight to the model, read the Research models category next. If the work you are writing is a final-year project, the Graduation thesis category sets out what each chapter is expected to contain.

Where to start. The post on the quantitative research process gives you the whole shape in one read, which is worth doing before committing to anything. Then read the posts on research questions and on hypotheses, because a hypothesis written loosely cannot be tested in the results chapter and you will not find that out until you are already there. The post on variable roles keeps you from drawing a model where one construct is quietly doing two jobs. The posts on primary versus secondary data and on choosing a design are the two to read before you start your methodology chapter, not while you are revising it.

name: Graduation thesis
intro_md:
A graduation thesis is the first time most students carry a piece of research from question to defence on their own, usually in a few months, usually alongside an internship or a full course load. What is missing is rarely the knowledge. It is the order: what has to happen first, what can run in parallel, and which dates cannot slip.

The posts here follow the five-chapter structure most departments expect: introduction, literature review and model, methodology, results, and conclusions with implications. Each chapter gets its own post covering what it has to contain, how to write it, the mistakes a committee reliably catches, and a few sentence patterns you can put your own figures into.

There are also posts on choosing a topic that fits your field, writing an abstract, presenting tables and figures so they can be read without the surrounding paragraph, citing in APA, and preparing for the defence. Anything that involves running numbers lives in the SPSS and SmartPLS categories, so the posts here can stay on how a result becomes prose.

A taught master's dissertation raises the bar on originality and on how far the model has to justify itself, but the chapter-by-chapter advice here still applies to one.

Where to start. With no topic yet, read the post on choosing one within your field, and the post on what makes a topic small enough to finish in a single term. With a topic settled, read the five-chapter overview so you know what each chapter owes the reader, then the post on chapter one, which is the chapter a committee reads most closely and students write most quickly. The posts on APA citation and on presenting tables are worth reading before you start writing rather than during revision, because retrofitting either one costs more than doing it right the first time. Leave the post on preparing for the defence until the last two weeks.

name: SmartPLS
intro_md:
Once a model has several latent constructs, a mediator or two, a moderator, or a sample too small for covariance-based estimation, regression in SPSS starts to strain and PLS-SEM in SmartPLS becomes the practical choice. That is why it turns up in so many management and marketing dissertations.

The posts follow the two stages of a PLS-SEM analysis in the order you run them. The measurement model comes first: outer loadings, composite reliability, average variance extracted, and discriminant validity by both the Fornell-Larcker criterion and HTMT. The structural model follows: collinearity with VIF, path coefficients and bootstrapping, R squared, f squared, Q squared, and then mediation, moderation, and multigroup analysis when the study calls for them.

Each post points to the exact place in SmartPLS 4, explains the results table it produces, gives its threshold with a source, and closes with a paragraph on writing that result into the results chapter. The troubleshooting posts cover the three problems that come up most: an outer loading too low to keep, an HTMT value over the limit, and a path that does not reach significance on the hypothesis you cared about.

If you are still choosing between PLS-SEM and covariance-based SEM in AMOS, one post compares them plainly, including the cases where PLS is the weaker option. Background on SEM and on the statistics underneath it sits in the Statistics category.

Where to start. Read the introduction to PLS-SEM and the comparison with CB-SEM first, so you are confident SmartPLS suits your model rather than that it was the tool with the most tutorials. Then follow the real run order: the measurement model post covering loadings, CR and AVE, then discriminant validity and HTMT, then the structural model with bootstrapping and path coefficients. The mediation and moderation posts matter only if your model contains them. Save the troubleshooting posts for the moment you hit the problem, since reading them in advance mostly teaches you to expect failures you may never have.

name: Research models
intro_md:
The research model decides everything downstream: what the questionnaire has to measure, how large the sample needs to be, which analysis is appropriate, and whether there is anything worth discussing at the end. A model chosen carelessly in the literature review cannot be repaired in the results chapter.

This category covers the theories and models that appear most often in management, marketing, and information systems research: TAM, the theory of planned behaviour, UTAUT, SERVQUAL, expectation confirmation, and the families of models around motivation, commitment, and behavioural intention. Each post gives the origin of the model with its original citation, the constructs and hypotheses it is normally used with, established scales for each construct, and the questions worth asking before transplanting a model into a context different from the one it was validated in.

Alongside those are posts on the ideas underneath: independent and dependent variables, mediators, moderators, control variables, drawing a model so that the diagram and the hypotheses agree with each other, and stating a hypothesis so that it can actually be tested.

Once the model is settled, the Surveys category covers turning it into an instrument and the SmartPLS category covers estimating it. If you are still choosing a question, start in Research methods instead.

Where to start. Read the post on variable roles first, since confusing a mediator with a moderator, or a control with a predictor, is the most common error in a first model diagram and it propagates into everything after it. Then pick a base model that suits your question: TAM or UTAUT for intention to use a technology, the theory of planned behaviour for behavioural intention more generally, SERVQUAL for service quality and satisfaction. The post on building a research model covers combining and adapting published models without losing the theoretical grounding that justified them in the first place. Read the post on writing hypotheses before you finalise the diagram, so that every arrow in it corresponds to something you can test.
